title: Mechanical Properties of Solids and Fluids
summary: Solids resist deformation: within the elastic limit stress ∝ strain (Hooke's law). Young's, bulk and shear moduli measure stiffness for stretching, squeezing and twisting.
In a fluid at rest, pressure grows with depth (P = P₀ + ρgh) and is transmitted equally in all directions (Pascal's law) — the idea behind hydraulic lifts and brakes.
Moving fluids obey continuity (Av = constant) and Bernoulli's principle (P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant). Viscosity opposes flow; a falling sphere reaches a terminal velocity (Stokes' law).
Surface tension makes liquid surfaces behave like stretched films: it causes excess pressure inside drops and bubbles and capillary rise.

formulas.name: Stress and strain
formulas.formula: stress = F/A (N/m²);  longitudinal strain = ΔL/L;  volume strain = ΔV/V;  shear strain = θ
formulas.note: Strain has no unit; stress has the unit of pressure.

formulas.name: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
formulas.note: ΔL ∝ L/A — a thinner or longer wire stretches more for the same load.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus and compressibility
formulas.when: Squeezing a body from all sides.
formulas.note: The minus sign makes B positive because volume decreases.

formulas.name: Poisson's ratio
formulas.formula: σ = (lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) = −(Δd/d)/(ΔL/L);  theoretical range −1 to 0.5
formulas.when: Change in thickness when a wire is stretched.

formulas.name: Elastic potential energy
formulas.formula: U = ½ × stress × strain × volume = ½ F ΔL;  energy density u = stress²/2Y
formulas.when: Energy stored in a stretched wire.

formulas.name: Pressure in a fluid at rest
formulas.mistake: Gauge pressure = ρgh (without P₀) — check which one the question asks for.

formulas.name: Pascal's law: hydraulic lift
formulas.mistake: Force is multiplied but work is not — the small piston moves farther.

formulas.name: Equation of continuity
formulas.when: Speed of an incompressible fluid in a pipe of changing area.

formulas.name: Bernoulli's principle
formulas.formula: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline
formulas.when: Venturi meter, aerofoil lift, blowing roofs, atomisers.
formulas.note: Valid for steady, non-viscous, incompressible, streamline flow only.

formulas.name: Torricelli's law (speed of efflux)
formulas.formula: v = √(2gh)  (h = depth of the hole below the free surface)
formulas.when: Water from a hole in a tank.

formulas.name: Viscous force and Stokes' law
formulas.formula: F = η A (dv/dx);  on a sphere F = 6πηrv

formulas.name: Terminal velocity
formulas.when: Rain drops, ball bearings in glycerine.
formulas.note: v_t ∝ r² — a drop twice the radius falls four times faster.

formulas.name: Reynolds number and critical velocity
formulas.formula: Rₑ = ρ v D/η;  streamline below ~1000, turbulent above ~2000
formulas.when: Predicting whether flow is smooth or turbulent.

formulas.name: Surface tension and surface energy
formulas.formula: S = F/L = (surface energy)/(area);  work to increase area W = S ΔA
formulas.note: A soap bubble has TWO surfaces — double the area.

formulas.name: Excess pressure
formulas.formula: liquid drop / air bubble in a liquid: ΔP = 2S/r;  soap bubble in air: ΔP = 4S/r
formulas.note: Use 4S/r only for a soap bubble (two surfaces).

formulas.name: Capillary rise
formulas.when: Liquid rising or falling in a narrow tube.
formulas.note: If θ > 90° (mercury in glass), h is negative — the liquid falls.

examples.title: Terminal velocity of a drop
examples.problem: A water drop of radius 1 mm falls in air (η = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s; ignore air density). Terminal velocity?
examples.solution: v_t = 2r²ρg/(9η) = 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 1000 × 9.8/(9 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 121 m/s (real drops are slower because the flow is no longer streamline).

topics.title: Stress–strain curve
topics.explain: Up to the proportional limit the graph is a straight line (Hooke's law). Beyond the elastic limit the body does not regain its shape; at the yield point it flows plastically, and at the breaking point it fractures. Ductile materials (copper) have a long plastic region; brittle ones (glass) break soon after the elastic limit.

topics.title: Applications of elasticity
topics.explain: Steel is more elastic than rubber (larger Y). Beams are made with an I-section to resist bending with less material. Crane ropes are made of many thin strands, and the maximum height of a mountain is limited by the elastic limit of rocks.

topics.title: Pressure facts
topics.explain: Pressure at a depth depends only on depth, not on the shape of the vessel (hydrostatic paradox). Atmospheric pressure ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 76 cm of mercury. A barometer measures it; an open-tube manometer measures gauge pressure.

topics.title: Buoyancy and floating
topics.explain: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes). A body floats when its density is less than the fluid's; the fraction submerged = ρ_body/ρ_fluid.

topics.title: Streamline and turbulent flow
topics.explain: In streamline flow the velocity at a point does not change with time and streamlines never cross. Above the critical velocity flow becomes turbulent and Bernoulli's equation no longer applies.

topics.title: Applications of Bernoulli
topics.explain: Aerofoil: faster air above the wing → lower pressure → lift. Roofs blow off in storms. Two boats moving side by side are pulled together. Atomisers and Bunsen burners suck in fluid where speed is high.

topics.title: Viscosity
topics.explain: Viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature; viscosity of gases increases with temperature. Unit: Pa s (poiseuille); 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s.

topics.title: Surface tension effects
topics.explain: Drops are spherical (minimum area). Surface tension falls with temperature and with detergents. Angle of contact < 90° → liquid wets the surface and rises in a capillary (water–glass); > 90° → does not wet and falls (mercury–glass).

ratta: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂;  P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant;  v = √(2gh).
Liquids: viscosity ↓ with T;  gases: viscosity ↑ with T.
